title: 〜さ (sentence-ending particle)
meaning: A casual sentence-ending particle for stating things lightly, often with a “that's obvious” or “no big deal” feel. It can also be used mid-sentence as a filler.
connection: Noun／na-adjective stem／verb・i-adjective plain form + さ

senses.label: Casual assertion
senses.meaning: States a conclusion lightly and offhandedly. The tone is relaxed, sometimes nonchalant or a little bit tough. Close to English “..., you know” or “sure”.
senses.connection: Noun・na-adjective stem + さ (no 「だ」); verb・i-adjective plain form + さ. Common: 「なんとかなるさ」, 「平気さ」
examples: It's fine. Things will work out.
That kind of thing? It's easy.

senses.label: Challenging question
senses.meaning: Used with a question word to push back or demand an answer with irritation. The tone is fairly sharp, like “What's so...?” or “Why do I have to...?”.
senses.connection: Question word + ... + さ／のさ. Common: 「何さ」, 「どうしてなのさ」
examples: What's so funny?
Why am I the only one getting scolded?

senses.label: Mid-sentence filler
senses.meaning: Inserted at a pause in a sentence to get the listener's attention or set the rhythm, like “so...” or “like...”. It has no real meaning. Overusing it sounds childish or sloppy.
senses.connection: Phrase・clause + さ、. Common: 「あのさ、」, 「それでさ、」
examples: Hey, can you listen to me for a sec?
So yesterday, I ran into my teacher at the station.

senses.label: Passing on hearsay
senses.meaning: 「〜ってさ」 reports what someone else said, in a light tone. Like “I heard ...” or “they say ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + ってさ
examples: They say it's going to rain tomorrow.
I heard Tanaka is quitting the company.

notes: After nouns and na-adjectives, attach 「さ」 directly. Not ✕「学生ださ」, but 「学生さ」.
This is very casual speech, used more by men. Don't use it with bosses or older people.
The 「〜さ」 that turns adjectives into nouns (「寒さ」, 「高さ」) is a suffix and has nothing to do with this pattern.

daily.title: Cheering up a friend
daily.description: A friend failed an exam, and you encourage them lightly.
daily.example: Don't worry about it. There's always next time.

daily.title: Starting a chat with a friend
daily.description: Opening a conversation with a close friend.
daily.example: Hey, are you free this weekend?

daily.title: Watching anime
daily.description: A male character speaks with confidence.
daily.example: Leave it to me. It's a piece of cake.

work.title: A senior comforting a junior
work.description: After work, in private, a friendly senior colleague comforts a junior who made a mistake. Not a formal setting.
work.example: Well, these things happen.

etymology: Its origin is debated. It is generally thought to have developed in the spoken language of Edo (Tokyo) from the early modern period, and it still sounds casual and breezy today.

similar.title: 〜よ
similar.explanation: 「よ」 tells the listener new information clearly. 「さ」 is more casual, with a light “isn't it obvious” feel, and doesn't stress informing.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: 「ね」 seeks the listener's agreement. With 「さ」, the speaker states a conclusion offhandedly without asking for agreement.

similar.title: 〜ぞ・〜ぜ
similar.explanation: 「ぞ／ぜ」 sound strong and forceful. 「さ」 sounds relaxed and cool, even nonchalant.

similar.title: 〜さ (adjective → noun)
similar.explanation: The 「さ」 in 「高さ」 and 「寒さ」 turns an adjective into a noun; it is a word-building suffix. The 「さ」 in this pattern comes at the end of a sentence or phrase and is a particle of tone.

title: 〜 (masu-stem clause linking)
meaning: In written Japanese, the masu-stem (continuative form) of verbs and adjectives is used instead of the te-form to link two clauses.

senses.label: Verb linking
senses.meaning: The verb masu-stem shows a sequence or a list of actions. It equals spoken 「〜て」 but sounds concise and formal. 「〜ている」 becomes 「〜ており」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 、 (行き, 食べ, し, 〜ており)
examples: I get up at six every morning and leave home at seven.
He graduated from university and got a job at a bank.
We are currently investigating the cause and will announce details at a later date.

senses.label: Adjective linking
senses.meaning: The 「〜く」 form of an i-adjective lists two qualities. It equals 「〜くて」. Common in descriptive writing and ads.
senses.connection: i-adjective minus い + く、 (安く, 広く)
examples: This room is spacious and gets plenty of sunlight.
The price is low, and the quality is good too.

senses.label: Nouns・na-adjectives
senses.meaning: 「〜であり」 links nouns or na-adjectives. It equals 「〜で」. The tone is formal; common in papers and speeches.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + であり、
examples: He is a doctor and also a writer.
This town has convenient transportation and is easy to live in.

senses.label: Negative linking
senses.meaning: 「〜ず」 means “without doing ...” or lists negatives. It equals 「〜ないで」／「〜なくて」 and has a strong written feel.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form minus ない + ず、 (言わず, 食べず; する → せず)
examples: He left the room without saying a word.
I went to school without eating breakfast.

notes: Mainly used in news, reports, papers, and formal speeches. Everyday conversation normally uses the te-form.
Tense and mood are set by the end of the sentence: in 「起き、出た」, 「起き」 is also past.
For 「いる」, the humble 「おり」 is common at the link: 「〜しており、」.
The linking form of 「する」 is 「し」, and the negative is 「せず」. Don't write ✕「しず」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news anchor reports what happened.
daily.example: Last night, a strong earthquake hit Tokyo, and many people were startled.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a series of a character's actions.
daily.example: She quietly stood up and looked out the window.

work.title: Writing a performance report
work.description: Listing several results concisely in a written report.
work.example: Sales increased over the previous year, and profits also improved.

work.title: Replying to a client's email
work.description: Explaining the current status and next steps.
work.example: We are currently looking into it and will contact you by the end of tomorrow.

etymology: The name 「連用形」 means “the form that connects to inflecting words”. In classical Japanese this form could already stand alone to link to what follows. Modern written Japanese kept this use, while speech switched to 「て」.

similar.title: 〜て (te-form linking)
similar.explanation: The meaning is basically the same. 「て」 is used in speech and ordinary writing; the masu-stem link is more concise and formal, mostly in writing.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: 「〜ずに」 modifies the following action: “do B without doing A”. 「〜ず、」 is more like a pause that lists two fairly independent clauses.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: 「ながら」 stresses doing two things at the same time. The masu-stem link shows a sequence or a list, not simultaneity.

title: 〜への・〜での・〜からの (particle + の)
meaning: Adding 「の」 after a case particle lets a direction, place, starting point, or partner directly modify a noun.
connection: Noun + へ／で／から／と／まで + の + noun

senses.label: への (recipient・direction)
senses.meaning: Means “to ...” or “for ...” before a noun. The noun is often a letter, gift, trip, or thanks.
senses.connection: Noun + への + noun. Common: 「〜への手紙」, 「〜への感謝」, 「〜への旅行」
examples: This is a letter to my teacher.
The number of people traveling abroad is increasing.

senses.label: での (place)
senses.meaning: Means “in／at ...” before a noun. It stresses where an action or event takes place.
senses.connection: Noun + での + noun. Common: 「〜での生活」, 「〜での経験」, 「〜での発言」
examples: I've already gotten used to life in Japan.
Please be careful about what you say in meetings.

senses.label: からの (origin・source)
senses.meaning: Means “from ...” before a noun. The starting point can be a person, a place, or a time.
senses.connection: Noun + からの + noun. Common: 「〜からの連絡」, 「〜からの道」, 「〜からの帰り」
examples: I read the email from my mother.
I don't know the way from the station.

senses.label: との・までの
senses.meaning: 「との」 means “with ...” and 「までの」 means “up to／as far as ...”. They work the same way as above.
senses.connection: Noun + との／までの + noun. Common: 「〜との約束」, 「〜までの距離」
examples: I had forgotten my promise with a friend.
Please tell me the way to the station.

notes: 「に」 cannot take 「の」: not ✕「東京にの旅行」, but 「東京への旅行」.
「が」 and 「を」 cannot take 「の」 either: not ✕「本をの購入」, just 「本の購入」.
Both 「東京の生活」 and 「東京での生活」 are correct; adding 「で」 highlights “there” as the place.
The 「との」 in 「〜とのことだ」 and 「〜との連絡」 introduces quoted content and is not part of this pattern.

daily.title: Showing a gift
daily.description: Telling your family who gave you the gift.
daily.example: This is a present from a friend.

daily.title: Talking about life as an exchange student
daily.description: An international student updates a Japanese friend.
daily.example: Life in Japan is fun every day.

work.title: Reminding a colleague
work.description: A boss reminds a team member not to forget a follow-up.
work.example: Please don't forget to contact the client.

work.title: Confirming the schedule
work.description: A secretary explains the meeting plan.
work.example: The meeting with the department manager starts at three.

etymology: Japanese case particles cannot modify nouns on their own. So the linking particle 「の」 is added to turn “noun + case particle” into a modifier, creating compound forms like 「への」, 「での」, and 「からの」.

similar.title: 〜に対する
similar.explanation: 「先生への感謝」 and 「先生に対する感謝」 are close in meaning. 「に対する」 is more formal and also often means “toward／against”, while 「への」 leans toward “directed at／given to”.

similar.title: 〜に関する
similar.explanation: 「〜に関する本」 means “a book about ...” and refers to content. 「〜への」 shows direction or recipient, not content.

similar.title: 〜との (quotation)
similar.explanation: The 「との」 in 「中止との連絡」 introduces content. The 「との」 in this pattern is 「と」 (“with”) plus 「の」.

meaning: Limits the angle of an evaluation: “in terms of ...” or “as far as ... goes”.
connection: Noun + の／plain form (+ という) + 点で（は）

senses.label: In terms of
senses.meaning: Limits the range of a comparison or evaluation. Often used to compare strengths and weaknesses. Adding 「は」 adds contrast: true in this respect, but not necessarily in others.
senses.connection: Noun + の点で（は）. Common: 「価格の点で」, 「品質の点では」
examples: In terms of quality, this product is better than other companies'.
In terms of price, this one is cheaper.

senses.label: In that ...
senses.meaning: A clause explains exactly which point. 「という」 can be omitted. Often paired with evaluations like 「優れている」, 「有利だ」, 「問題がある」.
senses.connection: Plain form (noun・na-adjective + だ) + という点で（は）
examples: Electric cars are drawing attention because they are eco-friendly.
When it comes to being convenient for commuting, this room is the best.

senses.label: Pointing out a feature
senses.meaning: 「〜点が」／「〜点に」 make a feature the topic and then evaluate it: “what's good／bad is that ...”.
senses.connection: Noun-modifying form + 点が／点に
examples: What's good about this plan is that it doesn't cost anything.
There are parts of his explanation that are hard to understand.

notes: Mainly used for comparing and evaluating. Common in writing and formal speech.
「その点では」 and 「この点で」 refer back to something just mentioned: “in that respect”.
In 「時点で」, 「観点で」, and 「地点で」, 「点」 is part of a compound word and is not this pattern.

daily.title: Choosing clothes
daily.description: Comparing two items of clothing with a friend.
daily.example: Design-wise, I like this one better.

daily.title: Choosing an apartment
daily.description: Explaining to your family why you chose this place.
daily.example: I chose this room because it's close to the station.

work.title: Comparing proposals
work.description: Comparing the pros and cons of two plans in a meeting.
work.example: In terms of cost, Plan A is better.

work.title: Product review
work.description: Pointing out remaining issues at a review meeting.
work.example: In terms of safety, there are still issues to address.

etymology: 「点」 originally means “a dot or mark”. It came to mean “a particular spot or point in something”, so 「〜点で」 means “on this point”, i.e. “in terms of ...”.

similar.title: 〜面で
similar.explanation: 「〜面で」 also means “in terms of ...”, but usually for broader areas (「経済面で」, 「健康面で」). 「〜点で」 is more specific and points to a particular feature.

similar.title: 〜にかけては
similar.explanation: 「にかけては」 is only used to praise someone's ability: “when it comes to ..., nobody beats them”. 「点で」 works for any evaluation, including negative ones.

similar.title: 〜に関して
similar.explanation: 「に関して」 means “about／regarding” a topic. 「点で」 shows the angle of an evaluation.

meaning: Draws a conclusion based on facts or analysis: “it can be said that ...”. The negative 「とは言えない」 means “you can't say that ...”.
connection: Plain form (「だ」 can be dropped after nouns・na-adjectives) + と言える

senses.label: It can be said
senses.meaning: States a conclusion after analysis or explanation. The tone is objective and measured, softer than a flat assertion. Common in writing and speeches.
senses.connection: Plain form + と言える／と言えます／と言えるだろう／と言えよう
examples: This can be called a great success.
Even by world standards, Japanese summers can be called hot.

senses.label: Can't be said
senses.meaning: 「〜とは言えない」 softly denies something: “it's hard to call it ...”, “you can't say ...”. Often paired with 「必ずしも」 or 「決して」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは言えない／とは言えません
examples: You can't say this method is necessarily correct.
The preparations can't yet be called sufficient.

senses.label: It could also be said
senses.meaning: 「〜とも言える」 rephrases from another angle. 「〜と言えなくもない」 means “one could say ..., I suppose” and is very indirect.
senses.connection: Plain form + とも言える／と言えなくもない
examples: You could also say that failure is the mother of success.
I suppose you could say his opinion is right too.

notes: 「〜と言えよう」 is written style, common in papers and editorials.
「〜と言えば」 introduces a topic (“speaking of ...”) and is different from this pattern.
「〜とは言えない」 is a partial denial and softer than 「〜ではない」.

daily.title: Talking about a friend
daily.description: Discussing with classmates who works the hardest.
daily.example: You could say he's the hardest worker in our class.

daily.title: Talking about a movie
daily.description: Giving a guarded opinion after a movie.
daily.example: I wouldn't call it interesting, but it wasn't bad.

work.title: Summing up a campaign
work.description: Reporting the results of a promotion at a meeting.
work.example: This campaign can be said to have been a success.

work.title: Writing a paper
work.description: Carefully stating a view in the conclusion of a paper.
work.example: From these results, it can be said that the two factors are related.

etymology: The quotation particle 「と」 + 「言える」, the potential form of 「言う」. Literally “can be called ...”, it expresses a judgment that has grounds.

similar.title: 〜と言ってもいい
similar.explanation: 「と言ってもいい」 is slightly exaggerated: “it's no exaggeration to say ...”. 「と言える」 is more objective and calm.

similar.title: 〜と言っても過言ではない
similar.explanation: This is the strongest: “it is no overstatement to say ...”. 「と言える」 just states a conclusion plainly.

similar.title: 必ずしも〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: 「とは限らない」 means “not necessarily”, allowing exceptions. 「とは言えない」 means “can't be called ...” and denies the evaluation itself.

meaning: Attaches to a noun to mean “... type” or “... model”. Used to classify things, people's personalities, or shapes.

senses.label: Model・version
senses.meaning: Shows a product's model, spec, or size. Common: 「新型」, 「旧型」, 「最新型」, 「大型」, 「小型」.
senses.connection: Noun・kanji element + 型. Common: 「最新型の〜」, 「大型の〜」
examples: I bought the latest model of smartphone.
A large typhoon is approaching.

senses.label: Types of people
senses.meaning: Classifies people by habits, constitution, or personality: “a ... type of person”.
senses.connection: Noun + 型. Common: 「朝型」, 「夜型」, 「血液型」
examples: I'm a morning person, so I go to bed early.
What's your blood type?

senses.label: Style・format
senses.meaning: Shows an activity or structure of a certain style or format. Common in news and business.
senses.connection: Action noun・noun + 型. Common: 「参加型」, 「体験型」, 「都市型」
examples: Participatory events are gaining popularity.
This class uses hands-on learning.

senses.label: Shape
senses.meaning: Shows that something is made in a certain shape. Can also be written 「形」.
senses.connection: Noun + 型（形）. Common: 「ハート型」, 「星型」
examples: I baked heart-shaped cookies.

notes: After a word it is read 「がた」. In 「典型」, 「模型」, 「原型」, 「類型」, and 「体型」 it is read 「けい」 and is not this pattern.
For shapes, 「形」 is also common (「ハート形」), still read 「がた」.
Add 「の」 when 「〜型」 modifies a noun: 「大型の車」.

daily.title: Talking about daily habits
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about your sleep schedule.
daily.example: I'm a night owl, so mornings are hard for me.

daily.title: Buying appliances
daily.description: Telling your family about something you just bought.
daily.example: I bought a new-model vacuum cleaner.

work.title: Product launch
work.description: A company introduces a new product at a launch event.
work.example: Next month, we will release a new compact model.

work.title: News report
work.description: A weather forecast warns about a typhoon.
work.example: A large typhoon is approaching Kyushu.

etymology: 「型」 has the native reading 「かた」 and originally meant a casting mold. It came to mean “a fixed pattern” and “a category”. After another word, the sound changes (rendaku) and it is read 「がた」.

similar.title: 〜風（ふう）
similar.explanation: 「〜風」 means “... style／... look” (「和風」, 「中華風」) and focuses on atmosphere. 「〜型」 focuses on classification and specs.

similar.title: 〜的
similar.explanation: 「〜的」 turns a noun into an adjective-like word (「経済的」). 「〜型」 is a noun used to classify things.

similar.title: 〜式
similar.explanation: 「〜式」 refers to a method, system, or format (「日本式」, 「自動式」). 「〜型」 refers to a type, model, or shape.

title: 〜ては・〜では (bad outcome)
meaning: Supposes a situation and follows it with a negative result such as “that would be a problem” or “that won't work”. Like “if ..., (it'll be bad)”.
connection: Verb te-form／i-adjective 〜くて + は; noun・na-adjective + では

senses.label: Condition → bad result
senses.meaning: Gives a condition and points out it leads to a bad result. The second part is often 「〜ない」, 「だめだ」, 「無理だ」, etc.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は (〜ては, 〜では); i-adjective 〜くては
examples: If you play games until late at night, you won't be able to get up in the morning.
When it's this hot, I can't get any work done.

senses.label: 〜ては困る
senses.meaning: Says you don't want someone to do something, voicing a complaint or request indirectly. Common: 「〜ては困る」, 「〜ては大変だ」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は困る／は大変だ; passive 「〜られては困る」
examples: We'd appreciate it if you didn't park your car here.
You really can't be late for the time we agreed on.

senses.label: Noun + では
senses.meaning: Takes the situation shown by the noun as a premise and draws a negative conclusion. Common: 「こんな〜では」, 「この〜では」.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + では
examples: With these grades, passing is impossible.
We can't play the match in weather like this.

senses.label: Casual 〜ちゃ・〜じゃ
senses.meaning: In speech, 「ては」 shortens to 「ちゃ」 and 「では」 to 「じゃ」. Same meaning, casual tone.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は → 〜ちゃ／〜じゃ
examples: If you drink that much, you'll ruin your health.
Staring at people like that is rude, you know.

notes: The second part must be a negative, unwanted result, never a good one: ✕「頑張っては合格できる」.
「〜てはいけない」 is a set pattern for prohibition; this pattern is a general condition plus a negative judgment.
The 「ては」 in 「〜については」, 「〜にとっては」, and 「〜としては」 is part of a compound particle and is not this pattern.

daily.title: A parent warning a child
daily.description: A mother warns her child who stays up late.
daily.example: If you stay up this late, you won't be able to get up tomorrow.

daily.title: Finding it too expensive while shopping
daily.description: Saying this to a friend after seeing the price.
daily.example: If it's this expensive, there's no way I can buy it.

daily.title: Telling a friend to drink less
daily.description: Urging a friend at a party not to drink too much.
daily.example: If you drink that much, you'll feel awful tomorrow.

work.title: A boss warning a team member
work.description: A boss warns someone who is often late.
work.example: You really can't be late for meetings.

work.title: Quality check
work.description: The quality-control lead makes a call on a defective product.
work.example: With quality like this, we can't send it to customers.

etymology: The conjunctive particle 「て」 + the topic particle 「は」. 「は」 singles out the condition and then passes a negative judgment on it, giving a “this won't do” tone.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: 「〜てはいけない」 is a fixed expression of prohibition. In this pattern the second part can be many kinds of negative results, such as 「困る」, 「無理だ」, or 「できない」.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 is a neutral condition, and the result can be good or bad. With 「ては」, the result must be negative.

similar.title: 〜ては・〜ていては（N2）
similar.explanation: The N2 pattern 「〜ていては」 stresses “if this keeps going on” and is more about continuation. This pattern is a general condition.

meaning: You can't avoid doing something because of duty, personal obligations, or common sense. Like “can't not ...” or “have to ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form + わけにはいかない

senses.label: Must, out of obligation
senses.meaning: You may not want to, but given relationships, your position, or common sense, you have to. It carries a feeling of “there's no way around it”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + わけにはいかない／いきません
examples: It's the wedding of a senior who has done so much for me, so I can't not go.
Everyone is helping, so I can't be the only one who doesn't.

senses.label: Forced by circumstances
senses.meaning: Because of the objective situation, you have no choice but to act.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + わけにはいかなかった (past), etc.
examples: The car broke down, so I have to take it in for repairs.
It was an important exam, so I couldn't skip it.

senses.label: Can't very well not ...
senses.meaning: Adding 「も」, 「〜ないわけにもいかない」 means “I'm not keen, but I can't very well refuse”, with stronger hesitation.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + わけにもいかない
examples: When someone asks me directly, I can't very well say no.

notes: The reason is usually personal relationships, position, or common sense, not purely laws or rules. For legal requirements, use 「〜なければならない」.
This is the opposite of 「〜わけにはいかない」 (can't do). Check whether 「ない」 comes before it.
It can be written in kanji as 「訳には行かない」, but kana is usual.

daily.title: A friend is moving
daily.description: A friend asks everyone to help with the move.
daily.example: It's my friend's move, so I have to help.

daily.title: Eating food someone made
daily.description: A friend went to the trouble of cooking something you don't really like.
daily.example: They went to the trouble of making it, so I can't not eat it.

work.title: A boss invites you out
work.description: The department manager invites you to a drinking party, and it's hard to say no.
work.example: If the department manager invites you, you can't not go to the party.

work.title: Handling a client request
work.description: A client makes an urgent request.
work.example: It's a request from a client, so we have to deal with it.

etymology: 「わけ（訳）」 means “reason／logic” and 「いかない（行かない）」 means “doesn't work”. 「〜ないわけにはいかない」 is literally “the logic of not doing it doesn't work”, using a double negative to mean “must do”.

similar.title: 〜わけにはいかない
similar.explanation: This takes the dictionary form and means “can't do”. This pattern takes the nai-form and means “can't not do”: the opposite direction.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: 「なければならない」 expresses general duties and rules. This pattern stresses psychological pressure from relationships or one's position.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: 「ざるを得ない」 is more formal and stresses “no other choice”. This pattern is more conversational and focuses on “it wouldn't be right not to”.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: 「ずにはいられない」 means you can't help it or can't control your feelings. This pattern means you rationally feel you must do it.

title: 〜たら〜た・〜と〜た (discovery)
meaning: A past action leads to discovering a situation, or to something unexpected happening. Like “when I did ..., I found ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form + ら／verb dictionary form + と, with the second part in the past tense

senses.label: Discovery
senses.meaning: After doing something, you find a situation that already existed. The second part is often 「〜ていた」 or 「〜だった」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ら、〜ていた／verb dictionary form + と、〜ていた
examples: When I got home, the package had arrived.
When I opened the window, it was snowing.

senses.label: Trigger → result
senses.meaning: After doing something, a result immediately follows. The result is beyond the speaker's control.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ら、〜た／verb dictionary form + と、〜た
examples: When I took the medicine, my fever went down right away.
When I pressed the button, the door opened.

senses.label: 〜てみたら
senses.meaning: 「〜てみたら／〜てみると」 means you found out only after trying. It often carries surprise.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みたら、〜た／みると、〜た
examples: When I went there, the shop was closed.
When I tried it, it was surprisingly good.

notes: The second part is an objective fact that already happened, not the speaker's own intention: ✕「家に帰ったら、勉強した」 (use 「〜てから」 here).
「〜と〜た」 is more written and narrative, common in novels; 「〜たら〜た」 is more conversational.
This “discovery” use cannot be replaced with 「ば」 or 「なら」.

daily.title: Waking up
daily.description: Describing to your family what you saw in the morning.
daily.example: When I got up this morning, everything outside was white with snow.

daily.title: Going back home
daily.description: Describing a visit to your parents' home.
daily.example: When I went home for the first time in ages, my mother had cooked a meal and was waiting for me.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes what happened to the main character.
daily.example: When I opened the door, a man I didn't know was standing there.

work.title: Checking email
work.description: Reporting to your boss that a reply came in.
work.example: When I checked my email, there was a reply from the client.

work.title: Checking data
work.description: Reporting a problem found during a check.
work.example: When I looked into it, I found an error in the data.

etymology: 「たら」 is generally thought to come from the classical 「たらば」 (the irrealis form of the perfective auxiliary 「たり」 + 「ば」). 「と」 is a conditional conjunctive particle. When followed by the past tense, both shift from a hypothesis to narrating an established fact.

similar.title: 〜たら (hypothetical)
similar.explanation: Ordinary 「たら」 sets up a hypothesis, usually followed by something in the future. In this use, the second part is a past fact: a discovery or result.

similar.title: 〜と (conditional)
similar.explanation: Conditional 「と」 shows a regular, inevitable result (「春になると花が咲く」). This use describes a one-time past event.

similar.title: 〜たところ
similar.explanation: 「〜たところ」 is similar in meaning but more formal and written, often used in reports.

title: 〜ように (as mentioned)
meaning: Placed at the start of a sentence, it introduces something the listener already knows or that was mentioned before: “as ...”.
connection: Verb plain form／noun + の + ように、

senses.label: As you know
senses.meaning: Introduces something the listener already knows as a premise. The polite form is 「ご存じのように」.
senses.connection: ご存じの／知られている／周知の + ように、
examples: As you know, the fees will change starting next month.
As is well known, Japan is a country with many earthquakes.

senses.label: As ... said
senses.meaning: Refers to something said earlier or by someone else, showing things are as stated.
senses.connection: 述べた／言った／言っていた／おっしゃった + ように、
examples: As I mentioned before, this plan has problems.
As our teacher said, keeping at it every day is important.
Just as the weather forecast said, it started raining in the afternoon.

senses.label: As shown
senses.meaning: Directs the reader to a chart or material. Common in reports, papers, and presentations.
senses.connection: 示す／示した／見て分かる／見る + ように、
examples: As shown in Figure 1, sales are increasing year by year.
As you can see from the graph, the population is decreasing.

notes: Usually placed at the start of the sentence, followed by a comma. The rest of the sentence matches what was referred to.
A more formal version is 「〜とおり」: 「ご存じのとおり」, 「前述のとおり」.
「遅れないように」 (purpose) and 「花のように」 (simile) are different uses; tell them apart by context.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with family about the weather in the morning.
daily.example: Just like the news said, it's really cold today.

daily.title: Bringing an umbrella
daily.description: Glad you listened to your mother.
daily.example: I'm glad I brought an umbrella like my mom said.

work.title: Internal company notice
work.description: Explaining a new system to all employees.
work.example: As you know, a new system will be introduced starting next week.

work.title: Explaining to a client
work.description: Repeating an earlier explanation in a meeting.
work.example: As I mentioned earlier, the delivery date is the end of next month.

work.title: Presentation materials
work.description: Guiding the audience to a chart during a presentation.
work.example: As shown in the materials, costs have dropped significantly.

etymology: 「ように」 is the continuative form of the auxiliary 「ようだ」, which expresses likeness. 「よう」 comes from the kanji 「様」, meaning “appearance／manner”, so 「〜ように」 means “in the same way as ...”.

similar.title: 〜とおり（に）
similar.explanation: 「とおり」 stresses “exactly as stated” and is more formal. 「ように」 is a bit softer and also common in everyday speech.

similar.title: 〜ように (example)
similar.explanation: The example-giving 「ように」 means “like ..., such as ...”. This use introduces something already known or already stated.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: The purpose 「ように」 means “so that ...” and usually follows a potential or negative form (「忘れないように」).

meaning: At the end of a sentence, it half-jokingly suggests a possibility: “maybe ...!” or “don't tell me ...”.
connection: Verb・adjective ta-form + りして (noun・na-adjective 〜だったりして)

senses.label: Light guess
senses.meaning: Casually throws out a possibility without being sure. The tone is relaxed, like “maybe ..., who knows”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + りして; 〜てたりして (〜ていたりして)
examples: Those two... maybe they're actually dating.
Maybe it'll snow tomorrow, who knows.

senses.label: Joking
senses.meaning: Says something unlikely, knowing it's a joke. Often followed by 「なんて」 or 「なーんて」.
senses.connection: Verb・noun 〜だった + りして
examples: Maybe I'm actually a genius.
What if I win the lottery? Ha ha.

senses.label: Worried guess
senses.meaning: Voices a possible bad outcome with some anxiety. The end is often drawn out or trails off with 「……」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + りして……
examples: Don't tell me I dropped my wallet...
What if the trains have stopped?

notes: Very casual speech, mostly among friends or in online chat. Not for formal settings.
The 「たりして」 in 「本を読んだりして過ごした」 lists actions (「〜たり〜たりする」) and isn't at the end of the sentence, so it is not this use.
It is like a lighter, more playful version of 「〜かもしれない」.

daily.title: Gossiping with a friend
daily.description: Whispering with a close friend about two classmates.
daily.example: Those two... maybe they're going out.

daily.title: Worrying about the weather
daily.description: Looking at the sky before going out and saying this to family.
daily.example: What if the rain never stops...

daily.title: Teasing yourself
daily.description: Joking when a friend compliments you.
daily.example: Maybe I could become a model, ha ha.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Coworkers casually chat about the boss over lunch, in private.
work.example: The department manager is in a good mood today. Maybe something good happened.

etymology: It is generally thought to come from the listing particle 「たり」 + 「して」. Originally 「〜たりして……」 gave one example; once the rest of the sentence was dropped, only one possibility remained, which gave rise to the sense of a light guess.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: 「かもしれない」 is an ordinary guess and can be used formally. 「たりして」 is more casual and playful.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: That 「たり」 lists actions. This pattern gives just one possibility and puts it at the end of the sentence as a guess.

similar.title: 〜なんて
similar.explanation: 「なんて」 is often used with this pattern (「〜たりして、なんて」) to mean “just kidding”.

meaning: Judging from signs, “if it looks like ... happens”, followed by a countermeasure, suggestion, or request.
connection: Verb・i-adjective plain form／na-adjective + な／noun + の + ようなら

senses.label: If it looks like ...
senses.meaning: Supposes a situation that seems likely and suggests how to deal with it. The second part is usually advice, a request, or an intention.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようなら. Common: 「〜ないようなら」, 「〜るようなら」
examples: If your fever doesn't go down, you should go to the hospital.
If it looks like you'll be late, please let me know.

senses.label: 〜ようだったら
senses.meaning: In speech, 「〜ようだったら」 is common. Same meaning, more casual.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようだったら
examples: If the rain gets heavier, let's call off the game.
If you're sleepy, go ahead and go to bed.

senses.label: 〜ようであれば
senses.meaning: In formal settings, use 「〜ようであれば」 or 「〜ようでしたら」. Common in business and notices.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようであれば／ようでしたら
examples: If the date is inconvenient for you, we will change the schedule.
If you have any questions, please feel free to contact us.

notes: The second part is usually a measure like advice, a request, or an instruction, not a plain description of facts.
Adding 「よう」 adds a sense of “depending on how things look”, so it is softer than plain 「なら」.
Don't confuse it with the farewell 「さようなら」.

daily.title: Looking after family
daily.description: A mother speaks to her child who has a cold.
daily.example: If you're not feeling well, stay home from school today.

daily.title: Arranging a pickup
daily.description: Making a plan with family on a rainy day.
daily.example: If the rain gets heavier, I'll come pick you up.

work.title: Customer service notice
work.description: A company adds a note at the end of an email to customers.
work.example: If you have any questions, please feel free to contact us.

work.title: Project management
work.description: A boss tells the team to report risks early.
work.example: If it looks like you won't make the deadline, please talk to me early.

etymology: The conditional form 「ようなら（ば）」 of the auxiliary 「ようだ」, which expresses likeness. 「よう」 comes from 「様」 (appearance), so it carries a guess: “if it looks like ...”.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「なら」 takes something directly as a premise. 「ようなら」 means “if things turn out that way”, with more of a guess and a softer tone.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 is a general condition. 「ようなら」 stresses a situation judged from signs, and the second part is usually a countermeasure.

similar.title: 〜場合は
similar.explanation: 「〜場合は」 states a condition objectively and formally, as in rules. 「ようなら」 carries the speaker's guess and concern.

meaning: 「〜かと思う」 offers a judgment softly; 「〜かと思った」 means “I thought ... (but it wasn't so)” or expresses surprise with exaggeration.
connection: Plain form (「だ」 can be dropped after nouns・na-adjectives) + かと思う／かと思った

senses.label: Soft judgment
senses.meaning: States your view in question form, sounding modest rather than assertive. 「〜かと思います」 is common in business.
senses.connection: Plain form + かと思います; 〜のではないかと思う
examples: I think this plan may cost a bit too much.
I think it might rain tomorrow.

senses.label: I thought ...
senses.meaning: 「〜かと思った」 means you thought so at the time, but it wasn't true: “I thought ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + かと思った／かと思っていた
examples: I thought you'd already gone home.
I was sure I was going to get scolded.

senses.label: Exaggerated surprise
senses.meaning: 「〜かと思った」 exaggerates a strong feeling at the time: “I thought I was going to ...”, “I nearly ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + かと思った. Common: 「死ぬかと思った」
examples: I was so scared I thought I was going to die.
I thought my heart was going to stop!

senses.label: Disapproval
senses.meaning: 「どうかと思う」 politely shows disagreement or doubt: “I'm not sure that's OK”.
senses.connection: 〜は どうかと思う
examples: I'm not sure that's a good way to put it.

notes: 「〜かと思います」 is softer than 「〜と思います」 and suits sharing opinions in meetings and emails.
「〜かと思うと」／「〜かと思ったら」 (“no sooner ... than ...”) are N2 patterns and different from this one.
「か」 can attach directly to nouns and na-adjectives: 「必要かと思います」.

daily.title: Getting a fright
daily.description: A family member suddenly appears behind you.
daily.example: You scared me! I thought you were a burglar.

daily.title: An unexpected encounter
daily.description: You thought your friend was already asleep.
daily.example: You're still up? I thought you'd gone to bed.

work.title: Giving an opinion in a meeting
work.description: Softly pointing out that the materials need changes.
work.example: I think this point may need revising.

work.title: Proposing a date
work.description: Suggesting a time to a client by email.
work.example: I think next week might be better. How does that sound?

etymology: The question particle 「か」 + the quotation particle 「と」 + 「思う」. The judgment is put forward as a question, so it sounds uncertain and soft.

similar.title: 〜と思う
similar.explanation: 「と思う」 states an opinion directly. Adding 「か」 adds a questioning tone, making it softer and more modest.

similar.title: 〜かと思うと・〜かと思ったら
similar.explanation: These N2 patterns mean “no sooner ... than ...”, with two events happening one after another. This pattern is a judgment or “I thought ...”.

similar.title: 〜のではないだろうか
similar.explanation: This also offers a view softly, but it is more written and common in essays. 「かと思います」 is common in spoken business Japanese.

meaning: Humble language meaning “to have the other person kindly do ... for us”. More formal than 「〜ていただく」.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + いただく; ご + Sino-Japanese action noun + いただく

senses.label: Having someone kindly do
senses.meaning: The other person does the action and our side benefits. Used to thank someone or explain what they did for you. Often followed by 「ありがとうございます」.
senses.connection: お〜いただく／ご〜いただく; 〜いただき、ありがとうございます
examples: Thank you all for coming today.
Our teacher was kind enough to come.

senses.label: Polite request
senses.meaning: 「〜いただけますか／いただけませんか」 is a very polite request. Used with customers, bosses, and clients.
senses.connection: お〜いただけますか／ご〜いただけないでしょうか
examples: Could you wait a moment, please?
Could you write your name here, please?

senses.label: Wish・request
senses.meaning: 「〜いただきたい」 and 「〜いただければ幸いです」 softly express that you want someone to do something. Common in letters and emails.
senses.connection: お〜いただきたい／ご〜いただければ幸いです
examples: We would appreciate it if you could check the materials.
We would very much like you to attend.

notes: Native Japanese verbs take 「お」 (お待ち, お越し); Sino-Japanese action nouns take 「ご」 (ご確認, ご連絡).
Common mistake: ✕「ご説明していただく」. Say 「ご説明いただく」 or 「説明していただく」.
「ご覧いただく」, 「お越しいただく」, and 「お召し上がりいただく」 are common set phrases.
The 「いただく」 in 「お菓子をいただく」 means “to receive／eat” and is not this pattern.

daily.title: At a shop
daily.description: A clerk asks a customer to wait.
daily.example: Could you wait a moment, please?

daily.title: Wedding speech
daily.description: The groom thanks the guests at the reception.
daily.example: Thank you all for taking time out of your busy schedules to be here today.

work.title: Requesting a check by email
work.description: Sending materials to a client and asking them to check.
work.example: Could you please check the attached materials?

work.title: Thanks at the end of a project
work.description: Thanking a partner after a project is finished.
work.example: Thank you very much for your tremendous cooperation.

etymology: 「いただく」 is written 「頂く・戴く」 and originally meant “to place on top of one's head”. From respectfully raising something above one's head to receive it, it came to be a humble verb for “to receive”. Combined with 「お／ご + masu-stem」, it forms an even more formal humble expression.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: 「〜ていただく」 works with almost any verb. 「お〜いただく」 is more formal and common in hospitality and business.

similar.title: お〜ください
similar.explanation: 「お〜ください」 is a direct request. 「お〜いただけますか」 uses a question form and is softer.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する
similar.explanation: 「お〜する」 is something our side does for the other person. 「お〜いただく」 is something they do for us; the doer is reversed.

similar.title: 〜(さ)せていただく
similar.explanation: 「させていただく」 asks permission for ourselves to do something. 「お〜いただく」 asks the other person to do it.

title: 〜お〜です (honorific)
meaning: Honorific language. 「お + verb masu-stem + です」 concisely describes someone else's action or state, roughly equal to 「〜ている」 or 「〜する予定だ」.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + です; ご + Sino-Japanese action noun + です

senses.label: Ongoing・state
senses.meaning: Shows that the other person is doing something or is in some state. Equal to 「〜ていらっしゃる」.
senses.connection: お〜です. Common: 「お待ちです」, 「お探しです」, 「お困りです」
examples: The department manager is waiting for you in the meeting room.
Are you looking for something?

senses.label: Having・knowing
senses.meaning: Shows that the other person has something or knows something. 「お持ちです」 = 持っている, 「ご存じです」 = 知っている.
senses.connection: お持ちです／ご存じです
examples: Do you have a parking ticket?
Do you know Mr. Tanaka?

senses.label: Plans
senses.meaning: Shows what the other person is going to do. Equal to 「〜する予定ですか」; mostly used in questions.
senses.connection: お〜です／ご〜です. Common: 「お帰りです」, 「お出かけです」, 「ご出席です」
examples: About what time will you be back?
Will you be attending tomorrow's meeting?

senses.label: Arrival
senses.meaning: 「お見えです」 and 「お越しです」 mean a guest has arrived; they are honorific for 「来ている」.
senses.connection: お見えです／お越しです
examples: Your guest has arrived.
The company president will be coming in the afternoon.

notes: Only for the actions of the listener or a third party, never yourself: ✕「私はお待ちです」.
Only a limited set of verbs work this way. Common ones: 「お待ち」, 「お持ち」, 「お探し」, 「お帰り」, 「お出かけ」, 「お急ぎ」, 「お困り」, 「ご存じ」, 「ご出席」.
「お疲れ様です」 is a set greeting and differs from this pattern's 「お疲れですか」 (“Are you tired?”).

daily.title: At a shop
daily.description: A clerk greets a customer who comes in.
daily.example: Are you looking for something?

daily.title: At the station
daily.description: A ticket inspector asks a passenger.
daily.example: Do you have your ticket?

work.title: Reception notice
work.description: The receptionist calls a colleague to say a guest is waiting.
work.example: A guest is waiting for you at reception.

work.title: Informing your boss
work.description: A secretary tells the department manager a guest has arrived.
work.example: Sir, Mr. Tanaka has arrived.

etymology: The honorific prefix 「お／ご」 + verb masu-stem (used as a noun) + the copula 「です」. Describing the other person's action as a noun avoids naming the action directly, which makes it sound indirect and respectful.

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: 「お〜になる」 is the standard honorific form and works in any tense. 「お〜です」 is more concise and mainly shows ongoing actions, states, or plans.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: 「お待ちです」 is roughly the honorific of 「待っている」, but it doesn't cover as many uses as 「ている」.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる
similar.explanation: Special honorific verbs replace the whole verb. 「お〜です」 uses a fixed frame to turn an ordinary verb into an honorific.

similar.title: お〜・ご〜 (beautifying)
similar.explanation: The 「お／ご」 in 「お茶」 and 「ご飯」 just make words sound refined. The 「お」 in this pattern shows respect for the person doing the action.
